vignette:
He remembers the rain that night—thin, persistent, glistening on the asphalt of the coastal highway. He was returning from a town hall meeting in a district he’d held for thirty years, his driver, Marco, humming along to an old jazz station. They were discussing the upcoming election, the shifting demographics, the need to connect with younger voters. Then the headlights of a delivery truck swerved into their lane. Marco yanked the wheel. The car spun, struck the guardrail, flipped. He remembers the sound of metal folding, the smell of gasoline, the strange quiet after the world stopped tumbling. He remembers Marco’s voice, thin and far away: “Sir? Sir, don’t move.”

That was eighteen months ago. Marco survived with a broken arm. He walked away with three cracked ribs and a concussion. But the thing that didn’t leave—the thing that followed him into every committee room, every fundraiser, every quiet breakfast with his wife—was the feeling that the world is a trap. He cannot sit in the back seat of a car without his left hand gripping the door handle, his eyes scanning the side mirror, his chest tightening until he can’t breathe. He stopped using his official sedan. Now he drives himself, even though his staff protests. He needs to feel the wheel in his hands. He needs to be in control.

The intrusive images come without warning. During a floor vote, he will suddenly see the rain-streaked windshield shattering. While shaking hands at a community center, he will feel the jolt of the impact, the seatbelt cutting into his chest. He has learned to mask the flinch—a cough, a glance at his watch, a sip of water. But the memories are vivid, tactile, relentless. He wakes at 3:00 a.m. drenched in sweat, the crash replaying in his mind, the sound of Marco’s voice calling his name. His wife, Margaret, reaches for him, but he cannot explain. He tells her it’s just stress from the session. She knows better.

He has become hypervigilant in ways that baffle his colleagues. At public events, he scans exits before he scans faces. He no longer stands with his back to a door. He refuses to ride in elevators alone. During a recent press conference, a reporter dropped a heavy camera bag, and he shouted, “Down!” The room went silent. He laughed it off, blamed the coffee. But his press secretary pulled him aside afterward and asked if he was okay. He said he was fine. He is not fine.

The avoidance is quieter but just as corrosive. He has declined every speaking engagement that requires travel by highway. He tells his chief of staff that he prefers trains for the working time, but the truth is that trains feel safer, more predictable. He stopped attending the annual Veterans Day parade because the route passes the spot where the accident happened. He fabricates scheduling conflicts. He cannot bring himself to say why.

His memory has frayed. He forgets names, misplaces papers, loses the thread of a conversation mid-sentence. During a debate, he stumbled over a policy point he had rehearsed a dozen times. His opponent smiled. His staff chalked it up to age, but he knows it is the fog—the constant low-level vigilance that exhausts his mind. He can no longer trust his own recall.

He is irritable. After a long day of votes and handshakes, he snaps at Margaret over small things—a mislaid pair of glasses, the volume of the television. He sleeps in the guest room now, because her presence startles him when he wakes from nightmares. He does not want her to see his fear.

At sixty-eight, he has spent a lifetime in public service, building a reputation for steady leadership. Now he feels hollowed out, walking through the marble halls of the capitol as if on a stage where the floor might collapse. He performs calm. He smiles. He shakes hands. But every car ride is a calculation, every closed room a potential coffin, every unexpected noise a return to that rain-soaked night. He has not told anyone the full story. He is a politician. He knows what it costs to show weakness.
